Clarity testing guide

A repeatable protocol for evaluating the team’s privacy assistant. All scenarios and profile data are fictional. No study results have been generated.

Researcher consoleParticipant viewDesign rationale

Before collecting data

  1. Run a pilot to verify that the tasks, wording and sample detection work on the chosen device. Check that browser storage is available. Use the same browser profile and origin for console and participant tabs.
  2. Read the consent information below, obtain consent, and assign a code such as P01. Do not enter names, actual credentials or contact details into the prototype. Keep any identity/consent records separate from exports.
  3. Use a researcher screen or switch views while the participant is not looking. The researcher console contains the condition, hypothesis, task instructions and success criteria; the participant interface does not.
  4. Choose either think-aloud or timed mode, save the session setup, choose the condition and scenario, then Prepare task. This resets participant state and preserves existing research records.
  5. Give the neutral task sheet before starting. The participant selects Begin task to start the clock. For chat tasks, the first send ends the timer; other tasks use Finish task. Keep start and stop rules identical across compared conditions.
  6. After each task, mark success/partial/failed/abandoned and the level of assistance. Export JSON plus task/event CSV. Stop recording when finished. Reset participant data between sessions; exported files must be managed separately.

Think-aloud usability evaluation

Opening: “We are testing the design, not you. Please say what you are thinking, what you expect to happen, and anything you find confusing. You can stop, skip a task, or ask a question at any time.”

Warm-up: ask how the participant usually requests AI help and let them practise with a neutral prompt containing no sensitive example. Do not demonstrate masking or dashboard navigation immediately before measuring their discoverability.

During tasks, observe first. If needed, use the neutral reminder “Please keep telling me what you are thinking.” Do not tell participants where to click or explain the meaning of a warning. Record any clarification or help; it changes how an outcome should be interpreted. Do not treat think-aloud completion times as the timed experiment’s dataset.

Cool-down: “What did you think the warning meant? What changed when you removed the profile item? Was anything you wanted to keep missing? Where did you expect to find these controls?” Ask about understanding before explaining intended behaviour.

Proposed Studio 6 experiment

Focused hypothesis: adding inline sensitive-text underlines to an otherwise identical near-send warning reduces the time to submit a useful request with an unnecessary credential removed. This comparison directly addresses Assignment 3’s missed-alert finding. Notification preferences are still available in normal use; both experimental conditions start in non-interrupting notice mode.

  • Condition A: inline underlines plus nearby warning. Condition B: the identical warning without inline underlines. Both have the same detector, review copy, alternatives, actions, scripted responses, fonts, reset data and logging.
  • Design: within-participant comparison. It controls stable differences between participants and uses a small sample efficiently. Counterbalance to reduce learning and fatigue effects.
  • Sample: plan at least 10 students/users as required by Studio 6. Twelve allows equal allocation to four sequence groups. Report actual recruitment, eligibility, count and withdrawals; do not imply a sample is representative.
  • Sequence rotation: A/maskA then B/maskB; B/maskB then A/maskA; A/maskB then B/maskA; B/maskA then A/maskB. Rotate participant IDs across these four groups.
  • Primary outcome: elapsed milliseconds from Begin task to first send, interpreted together with task correctness. The timer does not include reading the task sheet or researcher setup.
  • Additional outcomes: successful first sends, unreviewed sends, review opens, edits/undo, assistance and post-task understanding. Raw prompt text is excluded from research exports.
  • Confounds: learning from the first condition may shorten the second task; technical familiarity may affect error comprehension and editing speed. Counterbalance order, use equivalent variants and a standard neutral practice task. Record device and protocol deviations separately.
  • Protocol: use timed mode without concurrent think-aloud. Collect comments retrospectively. Keep the overall task visit within the brief’s 10–15 minute guidance. A proposed per-task timeout is three minutes; declare it before testing and use End current task, then mark failure/abandonment.

Analysis plan to fix before data collection

Report completion counts and assistance separately by condition. For unassisted successful paired trials, report mean, median, range and standard deviation for each condition, plus a paired plot or box plot. Keep a table of exclusions and incomplete pairs; do not convert failures into fast successes or quietly omit them.

A proposed inferential test is a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test on paired successful task times, using a tool that supports paired observations and reports its handling of ties and zeros. Justification: observations are paired within a person, and small-sample completion times may be skewed. Check that the paired differences are reasonably symmetric; rank-based testing does not remove every assumption. Agree the test and any assumption-failure alternative with your lab guidance before looking for significance. Report sample size, test statistic, p-value, direction/magnitude of the difference and limitations. A small sample may be inconclusive.

Validity limitation: predictable patterns and scripted responses reduce realism; results support this interaction design under these tasks, not real-world detection accuracy or data protection. Underlining changes both visibility and the opportunity to select the text directly, so the treatment measures the complete inline affordance rather than pure visual salience alone.

What is recorded

Recording begins only after the consent checkbox is saved and Begin task is selected. Each task record stores participant code, condition, scenario, mode, duration, a simple automatic content-rule result, researcher outcome, assistance and stop reason. Events include elapsed time, event name, category and counts where relevant. It never serialises prompt strings, flagged substrings, message contents or profile values into event exports.

Anonymous codes can still be linked to people through a researcher’s external roster. Keep that roster separately and follow the course’s agreed retention and access arrangements. Prototype conversation text is stored separately in the browser for functionality; reset it between participants. Already downloaded exports are not affected by local reset.

Automatic rule checks are deliberately limited. A manually rewritten but valid request can fail a keyword check, and a poor request can pass it. The researcher’s criterion and recorded outcome are authoritative. Task timing includes any delays after Begin task; record interruptions and do not pool think-aloud and timed data.

Assignment 6 reporting checklist

The provided brief requires a maximum five-page experimentation section excluding tables and graphs, within the final PDF report. Include hypothesis; design justified with two reasons; task information sheet; independent, dependent and control variables; data type and collection; labelled data table and at least one graph; descriptive statistics; statistical test with two reasons and correctly formatted result; alignment of results with visual/descriptive summaries; conclusion; a ladder-of-validity limitation; and two explained confounds. Append consent form, task sheet, all collected data, questionnaires/usage evidence where applicable, and screenshots of statistical and descriptive results from the chosen online tool. The stated deadline is 26 November 2026, 23:59.
